`public/models/helmet.glb` is now 7 MiB of GPU memory, down from 107 MiB, with a fidelity score of 0.94 against the original (the tool's recommended limit is 0.9). The file is also smaller on disk: 3.3 MB instead of 3.8 MB.

I built it with `node-assets optimize` using `--texture-format ktx2 --texture-size 1024`. The helmet's five 2048px textures are now 1024px KTX2, and the geometry is unchanged at 15,452 triangles.

I compared four candidates against `assets/helmet.glb`:

| Candidate | GPU MiB | File | Fidelity |
|---|---|---|---|
| Default (WebP 2048) | 107 | 3.1 MB | 0.959 |
| WebP 1024 | 27 | 1.2 MB | 0.879 (below the limit) |
| KTX2 2048 | 27 | 10.5 MB | 0.941 |
| **KTX2 1024 (chosen)** | **7** | **3.3 MB** | **0.940** |

KTX2 keeps textures compressed on the GPU, which is why it uses far less memory than WebP, which decodes to full RGBA. I went with 1024px because the 2048px KTX2 scores the same fidelity at four times the GPU cost. If you see softness on the visor or close-up detail on device, the 2048px KTX2 is the fallback, and that is one command to regenerate.

The output needs the KTX2 transcoder. Babylon.js loads it automatically, as you said, so the scene shouldn't need changes. I haven't loaded the scene on a Quest, so the headset result is still unverified.

The original `assets/helmet.glb` is untouched. The candidate files are in my scratch directory, outside the project.
